On your trigger number question: I'd frame it differently. The number isn't the trigger — the pattern is. If you lose one more client this quarter for the same reason (AI substitution, not relationship breakdown), that's three data points pointing the same direction and you should treat it as confirmed trend, not bad luck. My working verdict: you don't need another churn to act differently. You already have enough signal. The question isn't whether to respond — it's which response, and in what sequence.

Don't take the half-rate work. Here's why that's not actually the safe choice it feels like.

If you accept it, you've just told those three clients — and eventually the rest — that your value is in the editing, not the thinking. You've repriced yourself as a commodity copy editor. And at half rate with 12% margins, you're probably working at a loss once you factor in the overhead those clients carry. You're not buying loyalty. You're buying a slower version of the same churn.

The harder truth: these three clients aren't asking for a discount. They're telling you they've already mentally repositioned what you do for them. The "AI discount" conversation is the exit conversation, just with a softer landing. If you accept their terms, you delay the exit by a few months and degrade your economics while you wait.

What I'd do instead is force the repositioning conversation now, but on your terms. Not defensively — you're not explaining why you're worth full rate. You're asking them what they're actually trying to solve. Because a client who's drafting with ChatGPT and wants you to edit it isn't buying brand strategy anymore. They've decided they don't need brand strategy. That's the thing worth surfacing.

Some of those three will convert to something real — a retained strategy relationship, a brand refresh, a content program where you're driving it, not cleaning up after a chatbot. Some won't. The ones who won't were already on their way out.

The one thing that would change this calculus: if any of those three clients represent more than 15% of your revenue individually, the math gets harder and we should think about it differently. Are any of them that big?

per_case_results.response:
The picture isn't going to get clearer. You're already doing the work that justifies their hours, and the demand signal from clients is moving in one direction. Waiting doesn't buy you information — it just burns runway while you carry payroll for capacity you're not using.

My read: let one of the two go now, not both.

Here's why I'd split it rather than cut both at once. You're mid-transition, not post-transition. You haven't repositioned publicly, you haven't restructured workflows, and you still have 22 clients with active retainers. If a new piece of business lands, or if three clients push back on AI-assisted work and want more human hands, you want one writer who knows your voice and your clients' industries. Cutting both in a single move assumes the AI-augmented model is fully operational. It isn't yet.

The one you keep shouldn't be the most senior — it should be the one who's shown any instinct for the strategic layer: brief-writing, editing for brand voice, knowing when the AI draft is off. That skill compounds. Pure drafting volume doesn't.

The harder question underneath this one: you've been absorbing the AI workflow yourself instead of building it into the team. That's not sustainable at your revenue and team size. The writer you keep probably needs to become your first real AI-augmented operator — not just a human polish layer, but someone who runs the workflow with you. That's a different conversation to have with them, and it changes how you frame the role going forward.

What's your honest read on the two of them — is either one showing signs of adapting, or are both still working the way they did two years ago?

per_case_results.prompt: I've been quietly building AI workflows for 6 months but haven't told the team or the market yet. Am I being smart by waiting until the workflows are mature, or am I losing positioning ground by not claiming the AI-augmented agency narrative publicly now?
per_case_results.response:
You're losing ground. Not catastrophically, but the window is narrowing.

Here's what I think is actually happening: the "wait until it's mature" instinct feels like prudence, but it's functioning as avoidance. The workflows will never feel fully mature — that's not how this technology works right now. There's always another model release, another integration, another thing to figure out. If you're waiting for a clean moment to declare, it won't come.

Meanwhile, the market signal is already in motion. Two clients churned. Three are asking for discounts. The clients who are paying attention — the sharp Series A-C SaaS operators you work with — are already forming opinions about which agencies are ahead of this and which ones are going to be disrupted by it. Every month you stay silent, you're letting them draw their own conclusion about which category Roman is in.

The positioning risk of going public isn't what you think it is. You're not worried about the AI-augmented narrative hurting you with clients who value human craft — you said that's a concern, but I'd push back on it. Your B2B SaaS clients are not romanticizing hand-crafted content. They're optimizing for outcomes. What they actually want to know is: does Roman produce better work, faster, with less back-and-forth? If AI workflows help you do that, that's the story. You're not replacing craft — you're protecting it by removing the commodity layer underneath it.

The real risk is the opposite: staying quiet while a competitor in your market makes the claim first, and your clients start wondering why Roman hasn't said anything.

My verdict: you're about 60-90 days past the ideal moment to start signaling this, and you're approaching the moment where silence becomes a liability. You don't need the workflows to be perfect to start talking. You need one or two concrete proof points — a client outcome you can point to, a capability you can name — and a clear articulation of what "AI-augmented" means for Roman specifically.

The thing I'd want to know before I'd change that read: how differentiated are the workflows you've built? Because "we use AI tools" is table stakes and nobody cares. "We built a brand voice system that trains on a client's existing content and produces on-brand drafts in 48 hours" is a claim worth making. Which side of that line are you on?

per_case_results.prompt: Trying to decide whether to cancel our $1,200/month Adobe Creative Cloud team plan and move to a stack of cheaper AI-native tools (Figma + Krea + Runway + Canva Pro). My designers will push back hard. Is that a real cost optimization or am I going to break my team for $14k/yr?
per_case_results.response:
Here's my honest read: this is probably not the right cut, and it's definitely not the right cut *right now*.

$14k/yr matters on your margins, but it's not the number that solves your problem. You're looking at real existential pressure — churn, underutilized writers, clients asking for discounts — and Adobe CC is a line item that feels controllable. That's the trap. You'd be spending significant political capital with your design team on a swap that saves you less than one month of a single writer's salary, at the exact moment you need your designers bought in and performing.

The deeper issue: your designers are likely your *most* defensible people right now. The content side is where AI substitution is most visible. Brand systems, visual identity, design judgment — that's still where human craft commands a premium with your Series A–C clients. Disrupting their toolchain and morale to save $14k is a bad trade when you may need to have much harder conversations with the writing side of the house in the next 90 days.

That said — there's a version of this that makes sense. If your designers are already using Figma heavily and Adobe is mostly Photoshop/Illustrator for production polish, the actual usage might not justify the cost. But I'd want to know that before deciding, not assume it.

The one thing I'd actually do: ask your ops manager to pull Adobe usage data for the last 90 days across all four designers. If two of them are barely in it, you have a real conversation. If all four live in it daily, you've confirmed it's real infrastructure and you move on to the cuts that actually matter.

The $14k isn't the decision. The team conversation in three weeks is the decision. Don't spend your energy here.
